decks.module: Sign shapes and what they mean

cards.front: What kinds of messages do road signs give, and what previews the message before you can read it?
cards.back: Road signs preach rules, hazards, position, routes and services, and their silhouettes and hues preview the message inside.

cards.front: What does a downward-pointing triangle order, and what does a diamond-shaped sign warn of?
cards.back: Downward triangles order yielding at a sane pace with a halt if needed, while diamonds cry hazard ahead and beg caution with brakes at the ready.

cards.front: What does the eight-sided red sign always demand, where do you stop, and what comes after the stop?
cards.back: Eight-sided red always halts, demanding a full stop at the sign, line, crosswalk or curb, then deference to every crosser from both sides.

cards.front: What does each of the three shapes, the triangle, the diamond and the octagon, demand of a driver?
cards.back: Triangles throttle and sometimes halt for others, diamonds only preach caution for hazards, and octagons freeze every wheel outright, three shapes in rising strictness.

cards.front: What do rectangles and squares carry, how do tall and wide ones differ, and what do five-sided shields mark?
cards.back: Rectangles and squares carry orders, cautions and guidance, tall ones speaking law and wide ones pointing the way, while five-sided shields fence school ground and student crossings, their arrow plaques pinning the walk.

cards.front: Which sign shape alone marks school ground, and what does the posture of a rectangle tell you?
cards.back: Tall rectangles legislate while wide ones inform, and five-sided shields alone fence school ground, so posture plus corners name the duty.

cards.front: What do round signs foretell, and what do three-cornered pennants on the left rim of two-lane roads mark?
cards.back: Round signs foretell rails ahead and beg slower eyes and ears, and three-cornered pennants on the left rim of two-way two-lane roads open a marked no-passing stretch.

cards.front: How does the job of a round sign differ from the job of a left-rim pennant?
cards.back: Round boards foresee rails and summon eyes and ears, while left-rim pennants merely open a painted no-passing stretch.

decks.module: Sign colors and what they mean

cards.front: What do red, black and white, yellow and orange signs each tell a driver?
cards.back: Red signs always command obedience, from halts and yields to wrong-way bans, black and white ones either command or mark routes, yellow warns of road dangers and orange warns of work-zone dangers.

cards.front: How do the four colors red, black and white, yellow and orange pair up by job?
cards.back: Red always orders, black-and-white either orders or routes, plain yellow warns of the road and orange warns of its builders, four hues in two pairs.

cards.front: Where do green, glowing yellow-green, blue and brown signs each guide or guard?
cards.back: Green guides to places, roads and distances, glowing yellow-green guards walkers, riders and pupils, blue guides to roadside services and brown to parks and playgrounds.

cards.front: How do green, glowing yellow-green, blue and brown split by errand?
cards.back: Green points to places and miles, glowing yellow-green shields the vulnerable, blue sells roadside comfort and brown courts the outdoors, guide hues split by errand.

cards.front: What shapes and colors do rule signs come in, what do they script, and what marks a banned move?
cards.back: Rule signs stand square, tall or special-cut in white, red or black, scripting direction, lanes, turns, speed, parking and odd cases, with a red ring and slash branding the banned move.

cards.front: What does the red stop board with pale letters require, and what does the red-and-white downward triangle require?
cards.back: The eight-sided red stop board with pale letters freezes every wheel until crossers clear, and the red-and-white downward triangle throttles speed and surrenders passage to the busier road.

cards.front: Where does the red ball with a white bar bar entry, and what do wrong-way boards order?
cards.back: A white bar floating in a red ball bars every entry at ramps, crossovers and one-way mouths, and wrong-way boards mark the forbidden side of one-way streets and split highways, ordering a turnaround short of them.

cards.front: How do the four red rule signs differ: the octagon, the red-white triangle, the barred red ball and wrong-way boards?
cards.back: Octagon red demands the dead stop, triangle red-white only bends to busier wheels, the barred red ball locks whole entries and wrong-way boards punish the reversed, four reds of climbing refusal.

cards.front: Where do no-U-turn boards stand, and what do movement-ban boards veto?
cards.back: No-U-turn boards guard split highways and fast roads, while movement-ban boards veto lane or approach turns from poles or gantries, sometimes echoed by painted arrows.

cards.front: What do one-way, lane-use and keep-right boards each tell the driver?
cards.back: One-way boards chain drivers to the arrow’s heading, lane-use boards bless each lane’s allowed move, and keep-right boards steer wheels past islands, medians and mid-road blocks to the shown side.

cards.front: How does the scope of no-U-turn, movement-ban, one-way and keep-right boards differ?
cards.back: No-U-turn boards spare only the reversal, movement bans veto named lane turns, one-way boards jail the whole heading, and keep-right boards merely dodge mid-road blocks.

cards.front: What ground do no-passing boards mark, and when may a passing stretch be used?
cards.back: No-passing boards map sight-short ground where hills, bends, crossings and driveways hide entering cars, joining paint to open and close passing stretches that may be used only when safe.

cards.front: Who may use a wheelchair-marked stall, and what does a speed board post?
cards.back: Wheelchair-marked stalls belong to drivers holding disabled privileges alone, and speed boards post the fastest lawful pace for the stretch.

cards.front: What color and shape do caution boards usually have, what do they ask, and what do the signal-ahead and lane-shrink variants herald?
cards.back: Caution boards usually wear yellow with black ink in diamond cut, preaching slower wheels and ready brakes, with signal-ahead and lane-shrink variants heralding lights and merging funnels.

cards.front: What do walker-crossing boards with arrow plaques, flashing beacons and two-way boards each tell you?
cards.back: Walker-crossing boards with arrow plaques pin the footpath, flashing beacons guard busy unsignaled crossings, and two-way boards warn the divider is ending.

cards.front: What do school boards, slick-when-wet boards and stop-ahead boards each ask of the driver?
cards.back: School boards slow wheels near grounds and guards, slick-when-wet boards stretch following gaps and soften braking and swerving, and stop-ahead boards preview the octagon.

cards.front: What do zone-start boards ban, how do merge boards work, and what do small plaques beneath cautions give?
cards.back: Zone-start boards ban passing the cars ahead, merge boards fuse two lanes into one by mutual grace, and small plaques beneath cautions whisper the safe speed for the hazard.

cards.front: Which warning boards preview forced halts, which handle the merging funnel, and what do advisory plaques give?
cards.back: Signal-ahead and stop-ahead boards preview forced halts, lane-shrink and merge boards negotiate the funnel, and advisory plaques price the bend in safe speed.

cards.front: What do split-highway boards order, what do bend boards flag, and what do crossing boards with road names preview?
cards.back: Split-highway boards order right as roads fork one-way, bend boards flag curves and narrows, and crossing boards with road names preview junctions and forced turns.

decks.module: Guide, service and work zone signs

cards.front: What do arrow boards sketch, what sits below them, and what do guide boards name?
cards.back: Arrow boards sketch the coming bend with safe-speed hints below, and guide boards, mostly tall rectangles, name places, roads and routes onward.

cards.front: What do the shapes and colors of route shields reveal, and which road ranks do they show?
cards.back: Route shields wear shapes and colors that betray their road rank, interstate, federal, state, city or county, so map-planned trips follow them true.

cards.front: How does the job of an arrow board differ from the job of a route shield?
cards.back: Arrow boards sketch bends with safe-speed hints while shields wear rank in shape and hue, one reading the curve and the other the map.

cards.front: What rule do federal route shields repeat, and where do brown boards point?
cards.back: Federal route shields repeat the rank-by-shape rule, while brown boards beckon toward parks and playgrounds.

cards.front: What do blue squares offer, where do green boards aim, and how do mile ticks count?
cards.back: Blue squares hawk rest, fuel, camps and care, green boards aim at bike paths, lots, mileposts and chosen exits, and mile ticks march each mile from the south and west rims to reckon distances.

cards.front: What do the green information boards print?
cards.back: Ever-green info boards print borders, town lines, streams, heights and landmarks of passing interest.

cards.front: What do orange work boards warn of, what do detour boards open, and who rules the work zone?
cards.back: Orange diamond or square work boards warn of crews, slow detours, crawling machines and shifting pavement, detour boards open the backup path, and flaggers in bright vests with paddles and red flags rule the zone absolutely.

cards.front: How do green destination boards, green info boards, blue squares, brown boards and orange work boards sort by errand?
cards.back: Green destination boards aim at exits and miles, green info boards print borders and landmarks, blue squares sell services, brown beckons leisure, and orange work boards with flaggers rule the crew zone, color sorting the errand.

cards.front: What must a driver never do at the rails, and what is posted at every grade crossing?
cards.back: At rails, never race the train, never strand the car astride the tracks, spare the gearshift mid-crossing, respect the deceptive bulk and pace, and note the blue round-the-clock emergency number posted at every grade crossing.

cards.front: What does the round yellow X with black rail initials do, and what do the white crossed blades at the rails require?
cards.back: A round yellow X with black rail initials heralds the crossing from afar, and the white crossed blades at the rails yield wheels to every train like a yield board.

cards.front: Where gates and blinkers guard a crossing, when do you halt, how long do you wait, and who else must heed the signals?
cards.back: Where gates and blinkers guard, halt at the first flash before the arm falls, wait out the raised arm and dark lamps, never skirt the lowered arm, and walkers too must heed signals, gates, flaggers and officers.

cards.front: How do the yellow X, the white crossbuck and gates with blinkers rise in command?
cards.back: The yellow X warns from afar, the white crossbuck yields at the rails, and gates with blinkers jail wheels until arms rise and lamps die, three rail guards in rising command.

cards.front: What do portable or fixed message boards broadcast, and must a driver follow their directions?
cards.back: Portable or fixed message boards broadcast traffic, weather and hazard orders along the road, and every posted direction binds the driver.

recaps.module: Sign shapes and what they mean

recap_hooks.text: Signs give rules, hazards, position, routes and services, and the shape previews the message: downward triangles mean yield, diamonds warn, and the eight-sided red sign always means a full stop.
Tall rectangles give law, wide ones point the way, five-sided shields mark school ground, round signs foretell rails, and left-rim pennants open a no-passing stretch.

recaps.module: Sign colors and what they mean

recap_hooks.text: Red always commands, black and white either commands or marks routes, yellow warns of road dangers and orange warns of work-zone dangers.
Green guides to places and distances, glowing yellow-green guards walkers, riders and pupils, blue leads to services and brown to parks and playgrounds.
Rule signs come in white, red or black, and a red ring with a slash brands the banned move.
The stop board freezes every wheel, the yield triangle gives way to the busier road, the barred red ball bars entry, and wrong-way boards order a turnaround.
No-U-turn and turn-ban boards veto single moves, one-way boards set the whole heading, no-passing boards mark short sight ground, and speed boards post the fastest lawful pace.
Caution boards are mostly yellow diamonds with black ink that ask for slower wheels and ready brakes, and flashing beacons guard busy unsignaled walker crossings.
Stop-ahead boards preview the octagon, merge boards fuse two lanes into one, small plaques give the safe speed, and split-highway boards order drivers right.

recaps.module: Guide, service and work zone signs

recap_hooks.text: Arrow boards sketch the coming bend with safe-speed hints, and route shields, federal ones included, show road rank by shape and color.
Blue squares offer services, green boards aim at exits and print borders and landmarks, brown points to parks, and orange work boards with flaggers rule the work zone.
Never race the train or strand the car on the tracks, and note the blue emergency number posted at every grade crossing.
The yellow X warns from afar, the white crossbuck yields to every train, and at gates you halt at the first flash and wait for raised arms and dark lamps.
Every direction posted on a portable or fixed message board binds the driver.
